newsitem.title: USA: NHL-UNLIKELY HERO KOCUR THE TALK OF STANLEY CUP PRACTICE RINK.
newsitem.headline: NHL-UNLIKELY HERO KOCUR THE TALK OF STANLEY CUP PRACTICE RINK.

text.p: Joey Kocur was the hot topic of chatter at Stanley Cup finals practice after the tough guy became Detroit's unlikely Game 1 hero by scoring a huge goal in the Red Wings' 4-2 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers Saturday night.

Kocur, an enforcer or goon for his entire NHL career who was out of work at the beginning of the season, broke a 1-1 first-period tie by looking a lot like one of his far more talented teammates, rather than a guy who spends most of his time in the penalty box.
"From practicing with Joey we know he has good hands," said fourth line linemate Kirk Maltby after Sunday's practice session. "But he walked in there like (Steve) Yzerman or (Sergei) Fedorov."
On a goal that stunned the Flyers, Kocur stole the puck from from defenceman Kjell Samuelsson, put a move on Philadelphia goaltender Ron Hextall that got him off his feet and gave Detroit a 2-1 lead.
"I read how he was trying to clear the puck. I played a little snake in the grass with him and took a step and picked it off," Kocur said of the steal.
"I went around (Samuelsson) and was in on Hextall. I faked right, he went down and I went top shelf for the goal," Kocur said of his tie-breaker into the upper portion of the net.
Kocur said he felt no pressure when he found himself alone in front of the opposing goalie in the first game of the Stanley Cup championship series.
"A goal scorer might have gotten nervous because he is expected to score, but I didn't," Kocur recalled.
The 32-year-old Kocur, who despite a career of limited ice time has compiled well over 2,000 penalty minutes, considers himself to be very lucky to be where he is right now.

After some 12 seasons of protecting more gifted players and beating up people for a living for the Red Wings, New York Rangers and Vancouver Canucks, Kocur found himself a man without a team at the start of the 1996-97 campaign.
After failing to make the Red Wings in training camp, Kocur was out of the NHL and relegated to skating with has-beens and never-beens in the Detroit area.
"I knew I was near the end (of my career) and I didn't want to have it happen this way," he said.
"I went hard, got in shape," added Kocur, whose medical resume includes two battered hands from more than 150 NHL fights.
"I played some with the Red Wings Alumni and I got ice time in a beer league -- no hitting, no slap shots, but ice time."
Red Wings coach Scotty Bowman, owner of six Stanley Cup rings, happened to see Kocur with the alumini and then sent a scout to watch him in the recreational beer league.

With an eye toward a potential resumption of hostilities with the Colorado Avalanche -- bad blood and bloody clashes between the clubs that began with last year's Western Conference finals and continued into this season -- Bowman decided the Wings needed more toughness and signed Kocur on December 28.
"He gave me a chance," said a grateful Kocur, rubbing his knuckles from habit.

"I did what I had to to stay in the NHL," said Kocur, who finished last season with Vancouver. "I knew about the feeling between Detroit and Colorado and I think Scotty thought I might help against the Avs."

The Wings got past St Louis, Anaheim and the defending champion Avalanche in the first three playoff rounds without much of a contribution from Kocur, who had won a spot at right wing on the checking line with centre Kris Draper and left wing Maltby.
But in the opening period of the finals, the fourth line grinders stole the spotlight from the elite players.
Maltby opened the scoring, completing a short-handed two-on-one rush with Draper.
Then Kocur, who had scored a total of five goals in 97 previous career playoff games, silenced a stunned Philadelphia crowd with his unassisted goal.
"I was shocked when I realised what I had done," he admitted.
